SERMON BENEATH THE SUNK BELL: ON THE MARSH REVENANT

Attend, ash-brothers and ash-sisters. Draw close, but do not mistake
nearness for safety. The mud remembers the foot. The reed remembers
the hand. The drowned ground keeps its counsel until it rises to
speak.

I speak today of the Marsh Revenant.

Not as a beast for children’s warnings, nor as a mere corpse dragged
upright by foul water. The Marsh Revenant is a siege-breaker, and
this is its lesson: every wall believes itself eternal until
something comes that does not tire before it.

Look upon it in the mind’s eye. It appears as a corpse-like figure
burdened with marsh-wet decay, its every motion heavy with stagnant
earth. Yet beneath that rot lies the grim solidity of a breaker of
walls. It does not creep like a thief. It does not rage like a
beast. It advances with the weight of ruin made flesh.

Fortified resistance--hear those words and hold them tightly--does not
endure before it. The gate may be barred. The stones may be braced.
The defenders may gather behind their shields and tell one another
that stone is stronger than mud, that breath is stronger than
silence, that the living must outlast the dead.

Then the Marsh Revenant comes.

It comes without haste, and therefore without mercy. It projects
tireless, impersonal hostility. There is no plea to answer, no
bargain to strike, no wounded pride to soothe. It does not hate the
wall. It does not hate those behind it. It simply advances, as the
dead advance when summoned by no kindness and restrained by no fear.

And when it reaches the fortification, defense becomes desperation.

Remember this, not to surrender your gates, but to know what your
gates are for. A wall is not salvation. A barricade is not
deliverance. Defenses are tools placed in trembling hands, and all
tools fail when worshiped as gods. The Marsh Revenant teaches that
whatever is built may be broken, and whatever stands may be made to
kneel.

Yet do not call the creature cruel. Cruelty belongs to those who

choose. The Marsh Revenant chooses nothing. It is the revenant of
stagnant, hostile ground, and its silence is the silence of earth
that has swallowed too much. It advances with the inevitability of
the dead.

So watch the walls. Mend what may be mended. Guard the living. And
when the marsh begins to move, do not waste your last breath
declaring that it cannot.

The dead have never required our belief.
